(d) Earth pulls the apple downward

List-II
(i) Bullet pushes the gun backward
(ii) Ground pushes the foot forward
(iii) Nail hits the hammer with equal force
(iv) Apple pulls the Earth upward

Select the correct code:
1.x: Each reaction is equal and opposite: foot–ground pushes the foot forward, gun–bullet pushes the gun back, nail–hammer and apple–Earth, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
1.tq: Recall that the reaction reverses the direction of the action.
n: A foot pushes the ground backward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A gun pushes a bullet forward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A bullet pushes a gun backward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A hammer hits a nail. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The nail hits the hammer with equal force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The Earth pulls an apple downward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The apple pulls the Earth upward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The ground pushes the foot forward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Gun recoil results from the bullet pushing the gun backward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s: What happens to a gun when a bullet is fired from it?
o: It moves downward due to gravity
It moves forward with the bullet
It remains at rest in every case
1.x: The gun recoils backward. By the third law and momentum conservation, the bullet's forward momentum equals the gun's backward momentum.
1.tq: Recall recoil as a third-law effect.
n: A gun recoils when a bullet is fired. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s: The acceleration produced in the Earth by an apple pulling it upward is:
o: Always zero because the Earth is massive
Equal to the acceleration of the apple
Greater than the acceleration of the apple
1.x: The force on the Earth equals the force on the apple, but the Earth's huge mass makes its acceleration very small, not zero.
1.tq: Recall a = F/m; equal force on a huge mass gives tiny acceleration.
n: The apple pulls the Earth upward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The apple gives the Earth a very small acceleration. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Consider the following statements:

I. The total linear momentum of an isolated system is conserved when there is no external force.
II. The total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after the collision.
III. Total momentum is conserved for collisions of any type.
IV. The total momentum of an explosion remains zero if the system is initially at rest.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
1.x: All four are correct: without external force an isolated system's momentum is conserved in every collision, and an explosion from rest keeps total momentum zero.
1.tq: Recall the law of conservation of linear momentum.
n: The total linear momentum of an isolated system is conserved when no external force acts. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after the collision. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The total momentum remains zero after an explosion if the system was initially at rest. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Gun-and-bullet system during recoil
(b) Rocket-and-exhaust-gases system
(c) Exhaust gases during rocket propulsion
(d) Rocket during propulsion

List-II
(i) Gains forward momentum
(ii) Thrust arises from the momentum carried away by fast exhaust
(iii) Gains backward momentum
(iv) Total momentum stays zero because the system starts at rest

Select the correct code:
1.x: The gun–bullet system starts at rest so its total momentum stays zero, rocket thrust comes from momentum carried away by the exhaust, the exhaust gains backward and the rocket forward momentum, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
1.tq: Discriminate the whole system from its parts.
n: The momentum of the gun and bullet system is conserved during recoil. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The momentum of the rocket and exhaust gases is conserved. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Exhaust gases gain backward momentum during rocket propulsion. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The rocket gains forward momentum during rocket propulsion. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s: During gun recoil, the forward momentum of the bullet is:
o: Equal to the backward momentum of the gun
Greater than the backward momentum of the gun
Less than the backward momentum of the gun
Unrelated to the backward momentum of the gun
1.x: The bullet's forward momentum equals the gun's backward momentum, so the total stays zero as it was before firing.
1.tq: Recall momentum conservation for a system starting at rest.
n: The bullet's forward momentum equals the gun's backward momentum during recoil. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Consider the following statements:

Statement A: Vehicle safety design uses the principles of collisions.
Statement B: Jet engines use high-speed exhaust to produce a large momentum change.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
1.x: Both are true: collision principles guide vehicle safety design, and jet engines throw out fast exhaust to create a large momentum change and thrust.
1.tq: Recall the applications of momentum and collisions.
n: Vehicle safety design uses collision principles. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
High-speed exhaust produces a large momentum change in jet engines. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

Match List-I with List-II.

(b) Other units of work

(d) One electronvolt

1.x: The SI unit of work is the joule; erg, eV, calorie and kWh are other units; 1 J = 10⁷ erg and 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
1.tq: Recall the work units and their conversion factors.
n: The SI unit of work is the joule (J). [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The erg is another unit of work. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Sound, light, electrical, magnetic and nuclear energy are other forms of energy.
II. An LED or bulb converts electrical energy into light energy.
III. A nuclear power plant converts nuclear energy into heat and then electrical energy.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
1.x: All three are correct: sound, light, electrical, magnetic and nuclear are energy forms, an LED turns electrical into light, and a nuclear plant turns nuclear into heat then electricity.
1.tq: Check each energy conversion chain.
n: Sound is another type of energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Light is another type of energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Electrical energy is another type of energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Magnetic energy is another type of energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Nuclear energy is another type of energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
An LED or bulb converts electrical energy into light energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A nuclear power plant converts nuclear energy into heat and then electrical energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
How many of the following are examples of potential energy being converted into kinetic energy?
1. Free fall
2. A pendulum
3. A roller coaster
1.x: All three convert potential into kinetic energy: a falling body, a swinging pendulum and a roller coaster going down.
1.tq: Recall examples of PE turning into KE.
n: Free fall demonstrates conversion of potential energy into kinetic energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A pendulum demonstrates conversion of potential energy into kinetic energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A roller coaster demonstrates conversion of potential energy into kinetic energy. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Assertion (A): Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed.
Reason (R): The law of conservation of energy states that energy is transformed from one form to another.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
1.x: Both are true and R explains A: the law of conservation of energy says energy only changes form, which is why it cannot be created or destroyed.
1.tq: Check whether R is the law behind A.
n: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Energy can only be transformed. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
How many of the following demonstrate mechanical energy conservation?
1. A pendulum
2. Free fall
3. A spring-mass system
4. Ideal collisions
1.x: All four show conservation of mechanical energy: a pendulum, free fall, a spring-mass system and ideal (elastic) collisions.
1.tq: Recall the standard examples of mechanical energy conservation.
n: A pendulum is an application of mechanical energy conservation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Free fall is an application of mechanical energy conservation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A spring-mass system is an application of mechanical energy conservation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Ideal collisions are an application of mechanical energy conservation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: The SI unit of power is the watt (W), and one watt equals one joule per second.

o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
1.x: Both are true: power is measured in watts, 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹, and horsepower, kilowatt and megawatt are other power units.
1.tq: Recall power = work ÷ time and its units.
n: The SI unit of power is the watt (W). [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Horsepower (hp) is another unit of power. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The kilowatt (kW) is another unit of power. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The megawatt (MW) is another unit of power. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
One watt equals one joule per second. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

(b) Maximum static friction

List-I
(a) Walking or running
(b) Writing
(c) Holding objects
(d) Belts and pulleys

List-II
(i) Grip between pen and paper
(ii) Power transmission
(iii) Necessary for forward push
(iv) Grip prevents slipping
1.x: Friction gives the forward push in walking, grip between pen and paper, grip that stops objects slipping and power transmission in belts, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
1.tq: Recall the role friction plays in each activity.
n: Friction is necessary for forward push during walking and running. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction provides grip between a pen and paper during writing. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction provides grip that prevents objects from slipping. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction enables power transmission in belts and pulleys. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Grip is an advantage of friction. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Friction produces unwanted heat, which may cause overheating of engines and brakes.
II. Friction reduces the efficiency of machines by causing energy loss.
III. Friction opposes motion and causes extra fuel consumption in vehicles.
IV. Friction makes surfaces rough over time.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
1.x: All four are disadvantages of friction: unwanted heat, lower machine efficiency, extra fuel use and surfaces wearing rough over time.
1.tq: Recall the disadvantages of friction.
n: Friction produces unwanted heat. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction can cause overheating of engines and brakes. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction reduces efficiency through energy loss in machines. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction opposes motion. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction can cause extra fuel consumption in vehicles. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction makes surfaces rough over time. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Assertion (A): Centripetal force is a real force directed towards the centre of circular motion.
Reason (R): Centripetal force provides the necessary acceleration for circular motion.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
1.x: Both are true and R explains A: the inward centripetal force is real because it supplies the centripetal acceleration needed for circular motion.
1.tq: Check whether R gives the role that makes A true.
n: Centripetal force is a real force towards the centre. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Centripetal force provides the necessary acceleration for circular motion. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
How many of the following forces can provide centripetal force?
1. Tension
2. Gravity
3. Friction
4. Electrostatic force
5. Magnetic force
1.x: All five can supply centripetal force: tension (stone on string), gravity (satellite), friction (car on curve), electrostatic (electron) and magnetic force (charged particle in a field).
1.tq: Recall which real force acts in each circular motion.
n: Tension can provide centripetal force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Gravity can provide centripetal force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction can provide centripetal force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Electrostatic force can provide centripetal force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Magnetic force can provide centripetal force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

Consider the following statements:
Statement A: For a vehicle on a banked road, the component of normal force together with friction provides the centripetal force.
Statement B: In a loop-the-loop, gravity together with normal force provides the centripetal force.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
1.x: Both are true: on a banked road the normal-force component plus friction gives the centripetal force, and in a loop-the-loop gravity plus the normal force does.
1.tq: Check the forces acting in each case.
n: The component of normal force and friction provides centripetal force for a vehicle on a banked road. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Gravity and normal force provide centripetal force in a loop-the-loop. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
How many of the following statements correctly describe outward effects associated with centrifugal force?
1. Water is thrown outward in a washing machine.
2. Mud flies off a rotating wheel.
3. Particles move outward in a rotating frame.
4. The outward feeling on a merry-go-round is caused by a pseudo force.

7. Planetary rings and the shape of the Earth demonstrate outward effects associated with centrifugal force.
8. The Earth bulges at the equator.

n: Water is thrown outward in a washing machine. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Mud flies off a rotating wheel. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Particles move outward in a rotating frame. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A merry-go-round produces a feeling of being pushed outward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The outward force felt on a merry-go-round is a pseudo force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A centrifuge separates cream or blood. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Denser particles move outward in a centrifuge. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Planetary rings and the shape of Earth involve outward effects. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Earth bulges at the equator. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s: What is the primary function of gears in machines?

Conversion of kinetic energy into heat
1.x: Gears convert speed or torque, as in bicycles, clocks and cars. Perpendicular push is the normal force and restoring force is a spring.
1.tq: Recall the function of each machine part.
n: Gears convert speed and torque. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. A pulley is used for lifting heavy loads with cranes.
II. A pulley is used in flagpoles.
III. A pulley is used in elevators.
IV. Gears are used in bicycles, clocks and automobiles.

1.x: All four are correct: pulleys lift loads in cranes, flagpoles and elevators, and gears are used in bicycles, clocks and automobiles.
1.tq: Recall the uses of pulleys and gears.
n: Cranes use pulleys to lift heavy loads. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Flagpoles use pulleys. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Elevators use pulleys. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Gears are used in bicycles. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Gears are used in clocks. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Gears are used in automobiles. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
A pulley is used for lifting heavy loads. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Friction produces heat to ignite a matchstick.
Statement B: Friction produces heat in matchsticks and during drilling.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
1.x: Both are true: frictional heat lights a matchstick and also heats the drill during drilling.

n: Friction produces heat to ignite a matchstick. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Friction produces useful heat in matchsticks and drilling. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s: Newton’s second law is expressed as:

Statement A is false, Statement B is true

1.tq: Discriminate second-law from third-law applications.
n: Designing vehicles is an application of Newton's second law. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Rocket propulsion is an application of Newton's third law. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Walking is an application of Newton's third law. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Swimming is an application of Newton's third law. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Gun recoil is an application of Newton's third law. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Jet engines are an application of Newton's third law. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

1.s: While walking, which force acts on the foot in the forward direction?
o: The foot exerts no force on the ground
The ground pushes the foot backward
The foot pushes the ground forward
The ground pushes the foot forward
1.x: The foot pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes the foot forward, which moves the walker. This is Newton's third law.

The ground pushes a walking foot forward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
The ground pushes the foot forward. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:

o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

1.s:

1.s:
How many of the following are forms of potential energy?

2. Chemical potential energy
3. Nuclear potential energy
4. Thermal energy

Potential energy can be chemical. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]
Potential energy can be nuclear. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 38-44]

1.s:
Assertion (A): Without friction, people slip.
Reason (R): Friction is necessary for the forward push involved in walking.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
1.x: Both are true and R explains A: walking needs friction for the forward push, so without friction people slip.

1.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. A crowbar is an application of a lever.
II. A bottle opener is an application of a lever.

The force with which Earth attracts a body
The acceleration of a freely falling body
The force that keeps planets in orbit
2.x: Weight is the force with which the Earth attracts a body. Tides, free-fall acceleration and orbital motion are other effects of gravity, not weight.

n: Free fall involves the acceleration of a freely falling body. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Orbital motion keeps planets and satellites in orbit. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s: Which effect of gravity helps prevent the atmosphere from escaping?
2.x: Gravity holds gases near the planet, an effect called atmosphere retention. Tides and orbits are separate effects of gravity.
2.tq: Recall each named effect of gravity.
n: Free fall involves the acceleration of a freely falling body. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Orbital motion keeps planets and satellites in orbit. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Tides are caused by the differential gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Gravity prevents the atmosphere from escaping. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
Assertion (A): In a vacuum, all bodies fall with the same acceleration.
Reason (R): Free-fall acceleration is independent of mass.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
2.x: Both are true and R explains A: free-fall acceleration g does not depend on mass, so all bodies fall together in a vacuum.
2.tq: Check whether R is the reason for A.
n: All bodies fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum, independent of mass. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s: The acceleration due to gravity is always directed:
o: Away from the centre of Earth
Parallel to the surface of Earth
2.x: Acceleration due to gravity always points towards the centre of the Earth, which is why things fall straight down.
2.tq: Recall gravity as a centre-directed pull.
n: The direction of gravitational acceleration is always towards the centre of Earth. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. The value of g is maximum at the poles and minimum at the equator.
II. The value of g decreases with height.
III. The value of g increases with depth.
IV. Rotation of Earth slightly reduces g.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
2.x: I, II and IV are correct: g is greatest at the poles, falls with height and is slightly reduced by rotation. III is false because g decreases with depth, becoming zero at the centre.
2.tq: Check how g changes with latitude, height, depth and rotation.
n: The value of g is maximum at the poles and minimum at the equator. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
The value of g decreases with altitude. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
The value of g decreases with depth. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Earth's rotation slightly reduces g through the centrifugal effect. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
The equator has maximum centrifugal reduction of weight. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s: Which equation expresses the relation between weight W, mass m and acceleration due to gravity g?
2.x: Weight is mass times gravitational acceleration, W = mg, so it is measured in newtons.
2.tq: Recall W = mg from F = ma.
n: Weight is given by the formula W = mg. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
Consider the following statements:
Statement A: Mass is a scalar and remains constant.
Statement B: Weight is a vector and depends on location.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
2.x: Both are true: mass is a scalar measure of matter that stays constant, while weight is a vector force that varies with g from place to place.
2.tq: Discriminate mass (constant scalar) from weight (variable vector).
n: Mass represents inertia or the amount of matter. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Mass is a scalar quantity. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Mass remains constant. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Weight is a force vector. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Weight depends on location. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
Assertion (A): A body weighs more at the poles than at the equator.
Reason (R): The poles are closer to Earth’s centre and have zero centrifugal force.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
2.x: Both are true and R explains A: the poles lie closer to the Earth's centre and have no centrifugal effect, so g and weight are highest there.
2.tq: Check whether R gives the cause of A.
n: The poles have minimum distance from Earth's centre. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
The poles have zero centrifugal force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Weight at the poles is greater than weight at the equator. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
The value of g is higher at the poles because the poles are closer to Earth's centre. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
The equator has maximum centrifugal reduction of weight. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
How many of the following situations are associated with weight approaching or becoming zero?
1. Centre of Earth
2. Very large height
3. Inside a freely falling elevator
4. On the poles of Earth
2.x: Three are linked to zero weight: the Earth's centre, very great height and a freely falling lift. At the poles weight is maximum.
2.tq: Discriminate where g falls to zero from where it peaks.
n: Weight is maximum at the poles on Earth's surface. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Weight at the centre of Earth is zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
At very large height, weight approaches zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Apparent weight is zero inside a freely falling elevator. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
Assertion (A): Astronauts in an orbiting satellite experience apparent weightlessness.
Reason (R): The satellite and astronaut both accelerate towards Earth with the same acceleration due to gravity.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
2.x: Both are true and R explains A: satellite and astronaut fall towards the Earth with the same g, so there is no normal force and the astronaut feels weightless.
2.tq: Check whether R is the cause of A.
n: Apparent weight is zero inside an orbiting satellite. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
An orbiting satellite and its astronaut both accelerate towards Earth with the same g. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
Match the situation of weightlessness in List-I with its explanation in List-II.

List-I
 a. Freely falling lift
 b. Orbiting satellite
 c. Centre of Earth
 d. Deep space far from all masses

List-II
 i. True g = 0 because the pulls of the surrounding mass cancel
 ii. The floor no longer pushes up, so the normal force becomes zero
 iii. Gravitational pull becomes negligible with distance
 iv. Satellite and astronaut accelerate towards Earth with the same g
2.x: In a falling lift the floor stops pushing, so the normal force is zero; in orbit satellite and astronaut fall with the same g; at the Earth's centre true g is zero; and in deep space gravity is negligible, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
2.tq: Discriminate true zero gravity from apparent weightlessness.
n: At the centre of Earth, g equals zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
In free fall, the normal force becomes zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
An orbiting satellite and its astronaut both accelerate towards Earth with the same g. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Apparent weight N is zero when effective gravity is zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s: Which activity uses aircraft parabolic flights for weightlessness training?
2.x: Zero-g training uses aircraft flying parabolic paths, which give astronauts short spells of free fall.
2.tq: Recall how weightlessness is simulated on Earth.
n: Zero-g training uses aircraft parabolic flights. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
Consider the following statements:
I. Astronauts in space stations experience continuous free fall.
II. Microgravity experiments study fluid behaviour, crystal growth and human physiology.
III. Satellite instruments are designed for a weightless environment.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
2.x: All three are correct: astronauts in space stations are in continuous free fall, microgravity is used to study fluids, crystals and physiology, and satellite instruments are built for weightlessness.
2.tq: Recall the uses and effects of microgravity.
n: Astronauts in space stations experience continuous free fall. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Microgravity experiments study fluid behaviour. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Microgravity experiments study crystal growth. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Microgravity experiments study human physiology. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Satellite instruments are designed for a weightless environment. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s: What is the approximate altitude range of Low Earth Orbit (LEO)?
2.x: Low Earth Orbit spans about 160–2000 km; the ISS sits near 400 km. About 36,000 km is geostationary orbit, a trap.
2.tq: Discriminate LEO altitude from geostationary altitude.
n: A low Earth orbit extends from 160 km to 2000 km. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
The International Space Station is approximately 400 km above Earth. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
Match each orbit type with its description.

List-I
 a. Low Earth Orbit
 b. Geostationary Orbit
 c. Polar Orbit
 d. Elliptical Orbit

List-II
 i. Passes over the poles

 iii. 160–2000 km altitude
 iv. Approximately 36000 km above the equator with a 24-hour period
2.x: LEO is 160–2000 km, geostationary is about 36,000 km above the equator with a 24-hour period, polar orbits pass over the poles and elliptical orbits have unequal apogee and perigee, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

n: A low Earth orbit extends from 160 km to 2000 km. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

A polar orbit passes over the poles. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
An elliptical orbit has different apogee and perigee distances. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

n: An elliptical orbit has different apogee and perigee distances. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
A circular orbit occurs when centripetal force equals gravitational force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

n: The International Space Station is approximately 400 km above Earth. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:

Both Statement A and Statement B are false

2.x: Both are true: far from the Earth g and weight approach zero, and satellite instruments are designed to work in weightlessness.

At very large height, weight approaches zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Satellite instruments are designed for a weightless environment. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s: At which location is a body's weight maximum under normal conditions?
2.x: Weight is greatest at the Earth's surface; it falls going up, going down and in far space, and is zero at the Earth's centre.
2.tq: Recall that g peaks at the surface.
n: Weight at Earth's surface is maximum under normal conditions. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Weight at the equator is slightly less than weight at the poles. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Weight at the centre of Earth is zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
At very large height, weight approaches zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

Consider the following statements:
I. Weight is measured in Newton (N).
II. Mass is measured in kilogram (kg).
III. Weight can become zero in weightlessness, while mass remains present.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
2.x: All three are correct: weight is in newtons, mass is in kilograms, and weight can vanish in weightlessness while mass stays the same.
2.tq: Discriminate mass from weight.
n: The SI unit of weight is the newton (N). [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
The SI unit of mass is the kilogram (kg). [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Weight is zero during weightlessness. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s:
How many of the following locations are associated with weight decreasing from its normal maximum value?

1. Height above Earth’s surface
2. Depth below Earth’s surface
3. The Moon
4. Far space
2.x: All four reduce weight: height above the surface, depth below it, the Moon (about one-sixth) and far space where it nears zero.
2.tq: Recall that weight peaks at the surface and falls elsewhere.
n: Weight decreases with height above Earth's surface. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Weight decreases with depth below Earth's surface. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
A person's weight on the Moon is approximately one-sixth of the person's weight on Earth. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Weight approaches zero in far space. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s: Which of the following is studied through scientific experiments conducted in microgravity?
o: Differential gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun
2.x: Microgravity experiments study human physiology, along with fluid behaviour and crystal growth. The other options are effects of gravity, not research topics.
2.tq: Recall what microgravity research studies.
n: Tides are caused by the differential gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Gravity prevents the atmosphere from escaping. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Earth's rotation slightly reduces g through the centrifugal effect. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Microgravity experiments study human physiology. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s: When air resistance is neglected, the acceleration of a freely falling body is equal to:
2.x: Ignoring air resistance, every freely falling body accelerates at g, about 9.8 m s⁻², whatever its mass.
2.tq: Recall that free-fall acceleration equals g.
n: Free-fall acceleration equals g when air resistance is neglected. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

2.s: Which location on the Earth's surface is at the maximum distance from the centre of the Earth?
2.x: The equator is the point on the surface farthest from the Earth's centre because of the equatorial bulge of the oblate Earth. The poles are nearest, and the distance shrinks steadily with latitude.
2.tq: Recall the Earth's oblate shape with an equatorial bulge.
n: The equator has the maximum distance from Earth's centre. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

3.s:
Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(a) Floating or sinking
(b) Hydrometer/Lactometer
(c) Separation of mixtures

(ii) Average density controlled using ballast
(iii) Centrifugation, in which denser particles settle
(iv) Object floats if its density is less than the liquid density
3.x: A body floats if it is less dense than the liquid, a hydrometer measures relative density, centrifugation lets denser particles settle, and ballast sets a ship's or submarine's average density, giving a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii.

Centrifugation separates mixtures. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]

Ships and submarines control average density using ballast. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]

3.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The density of the atmosphere decreases with height.
Centrifugation separates mixtures because denser particles settle.
An object floats when its density is greater than the density of the liquid.
A hydrometer measures the relative density of liquids.
3.x: Option C is incorrect: a body floats when its density is less than the liquid's, not greater. The other statements on air density, centrifugation and hydrometers are true.

An object floats when its density is less than the liquid’s density. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]
A hydrometer measures the relative density of liquids. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]

3.s:

Statement A: Hydraulic brakes transmit pressure equally to all wheels.
Statement B: In a syringe, pressure applied at one end is transmitted to the other end.
o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false
Statement A is true, Statement B is false
Statement A is false, Statement B is true
3.x: Both are true and both show Pascal's law: hydraulic brakes pass pressure equally to all wheels, and a syringe passes pressure from one end to the other.
3.tq: Recall Pascal's law: pressure on a confined fluid spreads equally.
n: Hydraulic brakes transmit pressure equally to all wheels. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]
Pressure applied at one end of a syringe is transmitted to the other end. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]

3.s: The net upward force due to buoyancy is caused by:
o: Higher hydrostatic pressure at greater depth
Lower pressure at the bottom than at the top
Equal pressure at the top and bottom of a submerged object
The downward direction of buoyant force
3.x: Pressure rises with depth, so the bottom of a submerged body is pushed harder than its top. This pressure difference is the net upward buoyant force.
3.tq: Recall that hydrostatic pressure increases with depth.
n: Pressure at the bottom of a submerged object is greater than pressure at the top. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]
The net upward buoyant force is caused by higher hydrostatic pressure at greater depth. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]

3.s:
Match the buoyancy-related application with its role.

List-I
(a) Floating of ships
(b) Swimming
(c) Fish bladder
(d) Hot-air balloon

List-II
(i) Helps a person stay afloat
(ii) Controls buoyancy for depth regulation
(iii) Weight equals buoyant force
(iv) Heated air has lower density and produces a net upward force
3.x: A ship floats when weight equals buoyant force, buoyancy keeps a swimmer afloat, a fish bladder adjusts buoyancy for depth, and hot air's lower density lifts a balloon, giving a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.
3.tq: Recall how buoyancy works in each case.
n: Ships and boats float when their weight equals the buoyant force. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]
Buoyant force helps swimmers stay afloat. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]
A fish bladder controls buoyancy for depth regulation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]
Heated air has lower density in a hot-air balloon. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]
Lower-density heated air produces a net upward force in a hot-air balloon. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]

Soap bubbles have two surfaces. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]

Reason (R): They reduce surface tension.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
3.x: Both are true and R explains A: soaps and detergents lower water's surface tension, so it wets and penetrates dirt better and cleans more.

Soaps reduce surface tension. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]
Reduced surface tension gives detergents and soaps better cleaning action. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 92-96]

6.x: Diamond's refractive index is about 2.42 and its critical angle about 24.4°; its brilliance comes from TIR and dispersion, and facets are cut to maximise TIR, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.

n: Diamond has a very high refractive index of approximately 2.42. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Diamond has a very small critical angle of approximately 24.4°. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

A convex lens forms the image at infinity when the object is at F. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

6.s: Consider the following statements about Rayleigh scattering: 1. It occurs by particles much smaller than the wavelength. 2. Its intensity has an inverse fourth-power dependence on wavelength. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
6.x: Both are correct: Rayleigh scattering is by particles much smaller than the wavelength, and its intensity varies as 1/λ⁴, so blue scatters far more than red.
6.tq: Recall the 1/λ⁴ law for small-particle scattering.
n: Rayleigh scattering is produced by particles much smaller than the wavelength. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Rayleigh scattering varies as 1/λ⁴. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

6.s: A medium having a higher refractive index is described as:
6.x: A medium with a higher refractive index is optically denser, so light travels more slowly in it. Optical density differs from opacity.
6.tq: Discriminate optical density from mass density and opacity.
n: A medium with a higher refractive index is optically denser. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

6.s:
How many of the following statements are correctly associated with Mie scattering?

1. It occurs by larger particles.
2. Clouds produce Mie scattering.
3. Milk produces Mie scattering.
4. Mie scattering produces white clouds.
6.x: All four are correct: Mie scattering is by larger particles such as cloud droplets and milk fat, and it scatters all colours equally, making clouds white.
6.tq: Discriminate Mie (white) from Rayleigh (blue) scattering.
n: Mie scattering is produced by larger particles. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Clouds produce Mie scattering. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Milk produces Mie scattering. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Scattering produces white clouds. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

6.s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Rayleigh scattering produces a red sunset.
II. Blue or violet is scattered most because it has the highest frequency.
III. The human eye is more sensitive to blue than violet.
IV. The sky appears blue because the human eye is more sensitive to blue than violet.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
6.x: All four are correct: Rayleigh scattering reddens sunsets, high-frequency blue and violet scatter most, and the sky looks blue rather than violet because the eye is more sensitive to blue.
6.tq: Recall why the sky is blue and not violet.
n: Scattering produces a blue sky. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Scattering produces a red sunset. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Blue and violet are scattered the most in the atmosphere. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Blue and violet have the highest frequencies among the relevant visible colours. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
The human eye is more sensitive to blue than violet. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
The sky therefore appears blue to the human eye. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
A blue sky and red sunset are caused by Rayleigh scattering. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Shorter wavelengths scatter more strongly. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

6.s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Scattered light reaches the eye from all directions.
II. Sunlight travels a greater distance through the atmosphere at sunset.
III. Most blue light is scattered away at sunset.
IV. Red or orange remaining light reaches the eye at sunset, and pollution or dust enhances the red colour.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
6.x: All four are correct: scattered light comes from every direction, at sunset light's long path scatters away blue, leaving red and orange, and dust deepens the red.
6.tq: Recall why sunsets look red.
n: Scattered light reaches the eye from all directions. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Sunlight travels a greater distance through the atmosphere at sunset. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Blue light is scattered away during sunset. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
The remaining red or orange light reaches the eye at sunset. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Pollution and dust enhance the red colour of a sunset. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Shorter wavelengths scatter more strongly. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

6.s:
Assertion (A): Atmospheric refraction is caused by continuous changes in refractive index.
Reason (R): These changes in refractive index occur due to variations in air density.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

A is false, but R is true
6.x: Both are true and R explains A: changes in air density give changes in refractive index, which bend light gradually.

Air-density variations cause continuous changes in refractive index. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

6.s:
How many of the following statements about atmospheric refraction are correct?
1. It bends starlight randomly.
2. It causes the apparent position of a star to change.
3. It causes apparent stellar intensity to fluctuate.
6.x: All three are correct: atmospheric refraction bends starlight at random, shifting stars' apparent positions and making their brightness flicker, which is twinkling.
6.tq: Recall atmospheric refraction as the cause of twinkling.
n: Atmospheric refraction bends starlight randomly. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Atmospheric refraction causes random apparent positions of stars. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
The apparent intensity of a star fluctuates during twinkling. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

6.s: Atmospheric refraction causes approximately which of the following effects?
o: Two minutes of delayed sunrise or advance sunset
Two minutes of advance sunrise only
Two minutes of advance sunrise or delayed sunset
Two minutes of delayed sunset only
6.x: Refraction bends sunlight over the horizon, so the Sun appears about two minutes before actual sunrise and stays about two minutes after sunset.
6.tq: Recall advance sunrise and delayed sunset.
n: Advance sunrise is caused by atmospheric refraction. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Delayed sunset is caused by atmospheric refraction. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Atmospheric refraction accounts for approximately two minutes of advance sunrise or delayed sunset. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]

o: Both Statement A and Statement B are true
Both Statement A and Statement B are false

6.x: Both are true: atmospheric refraction shifts stars' apparent positions, and Rayleigh scattering gives the blue sky and red sunset.
6.tq: Discriminate refraction effects from scattering effects.

Statement A is false, Statement B is true

I. For General Category States, the Centre contributes 75% and the State contributes 25% to the SDRF.
II. For Special Category States, including NE and Himalayan States, the Centre contributes 90% and the State contributes 10%.
III. Up to 10% of the SDRF may be used for state-specific disasters not included in the notified list.
IV. The SDRF can be used for long-term reconstruction.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
62.x: I, II and III are correct: the Centre pays 75% of the SDRF for general States and 90% for special-category States, and up to 10% may go to State-specific disasters. IV is false because the SDRF is not for long-term reconstruction.

For general-category states, the state contributes 25% to the State Disaster Response Fund. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-50]
For special-category states, the Centre contributes 90% to the State Disaster Response Fund. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-50]

Up to 10% of the State Disaster Response Fund can be used for state-specific disasters. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-50]

The State Disaster Response Fund can be used only for immediate relief. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-50]

62.s: According to the Disaster Management Act, 2005, mitigation refers to measures aimed at:
o: Providing relief only after a disaster has occurred
Reducing the risk, impact or effects of a disaster or threatening disaster situation
Restricting disaster management to structural constructions
62.x: Under the DM Act, mitigation means measures to reduce the risk, impact or effects of a disaster or threatening disaster. The other options narrow or distort it.
62.tq: Recall the DM Act's definition of mitigation.
n: Mitigation consists of measures aimed at reducing the risk, impact or effects of a disaster or threatening disaster situation. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 30-32]

The maximum human-life loss in Andhra Pradesh occurred during the 1977 Cyclone.
